studies.label: Randomized feedback-sequence crossover: product improvement

counts_source.quote: Hence, the final sample size of 62 participants provided adequate statistical power for the primary analyses, though correlational results should be interpreted with caution due to slightly reduced power.

arms.name: Standard GenAI feedback (ChatGPT-4)
arms.description: General-purpose ChatGPT-4 supplies open-ended responses to general prompts and permits unstructured exploration. All participants experienced this condition in the crossover. The paper prints an overall final sample but no separate condition-specific analyzed count. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 169), GenAI feedback conditions; PDF pp. 8-9 (printed pp. 172-173), Procedure and Figure 3.

arms.name: Personalised GenAI feedback (Mr. Ranedeer)
arms.description: GPT-4-based Mr. Ranedeer uses configured learner preferences to generate a personalised learning plan and adapt feedback, including heuristic questions and substantive improvement suggestions. All participants experienced this condition in the crossover. The paper prints an overall final sample but no separate condition-specific analyzed count. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 169), GenAI feedback conditions; PDF pp. 8-9 (printed pp. 172-173), Procedure and Figure 3; Appendix Tables A1-A2, PDF pp. 20-21 (printed pp. 184-185).

studies.task: Chinese university students proposed three original and useful improvements for each of two everyday products, a stuffed bunny and a portable coffee maker, using the assigned GenAI system and submitting final responses in Microsoft Word (PDF pp. 7-8, printed pp. 171-172, Measures and Procedure).

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT-4 (standard feedback) and Mr. Ranedeer (personalised feedback), both based on GPT-4 architecture
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 169), GenAI feedback conditions. Exact model snapshot and release year are not stated.

preregistration.where: No preregistration or registered primary outcome is identified in the article or its appendix.

studies.shared_sample: Probable shared sample with c041, Effects of Personalized Generative AI on Student Creativity: Evidence from Creative Performance, Self-efficacy, and Attention Allocation (DOI 10.1007/978-981-95-4499-8_31), as flagged in forms/c246.json, sample_overlap. The screening form identifies matching demographics, methods, task timings, and all creativity means/SDs; it also states that neither paper explicitly confirms participant reuse or the exact overlap. Retain this as probable duplicate-sample evidence, not a confirmed shared-person count.

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Originality reflects the novelty of the solutions. Two trained raters, blinded to condition, independently rated all solutions on a five-point Likert scale from worst to best; solutions were presented in randomised order, and final scores were averaged across raters. Expert credentials and aggregation across solutions are not stated (PDF p. 8, printed p. 172, CPS performance).

sources.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 175), Table 2, Originality row; columns are Standard mean (SD), Personalised mean (SD), z, p, Cohen’s r, and its confidence interval
PDF p. 11 (printed p. 175), Table 2, confidence-interval column header

estimates.notes: The test is the reported z statistic from a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank comparison (PDF p. 10, printed p. 174, Data analysis). The paper does not identify the observation represented by each analyzed score or its SD; averaging across raters alone does not establish participant-level aggregation. No outcome-specific valid-pair counts are printed, so n_treatment, n_control and n_total are null despite the separately documented overall final sample. Cohen’s r and z retain their printed negative signs without recoding. The interval limits in paper_effect are for Cohen’s r, with confidence level in ci_level; no mean-difference interval is printed. Higher ratings represent more originality, task-appropriate quality or elaboration for the respective dimension. No first-round result is available.

not_extracted.reason: Self-reported confidence measured before each task and used as a covariate; not scored on produced creative output. PDF p. 8 (printed p. 172), Self-efficacy; PDF p. 10 (printed p. 174), Data analysis.
Time spent completing the task is a process/productivity measure, not creativity or diversity scored on the submitted solutions. PDF p. 8 (printed p. 172), Procedure.

Frequency of ignoring AI feedback, coded from responses to feedback during task revision. It measures engagement with feedback rather than creativity or diversity of final output. PDF p. 9 (printed p. 173), Feedback uptake; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 175), Table 3.

Frequency of directly copying AI feedback, coded from responses to feedback during task revision. It is an uptake measure, not a diversity comparison across people or a creativity score on final output. PDF p. 9 (printed p. 173), Feedback uptake; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 175), Table 3.

Frequency of applying AI feedback, coded from responses to feedback during task revision. It measures uptake behaviour rather than rated creativity or the number of ideas in final output. PDF p. 9 (printed p. 173), Feedback uptake; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 175), Table 3.

Total frequency of coded uptake events is an engagement/process measure, not a creativity or diversity score on produced solutions. PDF p. 9 (printed p. 173), Feedback uptake; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 175), Table 3.

not_extracted.what: Interaction-behaviour frequencies: CT1, CT2, CT3, TI1, TI2, TI3, TI4, I and Total
not_extracted.reason: These count coded conversational behaviours, including ideation-related interactions, task coordination and irrelevant discourse. They are process codes rather than creativity ratings or counts of distinct final ideas. PDF pp. 9-10 (printed pp. 173-174), Interaction behaviours and Table 1; PDF p. 13 (printed p. 177), Table 7.

not_extracted.what: Lag-sequential associations between interaction behaviours and feedback uptake
not_extracted.reason: Within-condition behavioural transitions and their associations with feedback uptake are process analyses, not randomized contrasts on the creativity or diversity of produced output. PDF p. 10 (printed p. 174), Data analysis; PDF p. 13 (printed p. 177), Figure 4 and accompanying text.

not_extracted.what: Correlations between feedback uptake and quality, elaboration or originality within each AI condition
not_extracted.reason: Associations with nonrandomized, post-assignment feedback-uptake behaviours do not estimate a contrast between randomized AI conditions. PDF p. 12 (printed p. 176), Table 4.

not_extracted.what: Backward regressions predicting quality, elaboration or originality from feedback uptake within each AI condition
not_extracted.reason: These model post-assignment uptake predictors separately within conditions and include covariates; their coefficients are not randomized AI-configuration effects. Model summaries and predictor coefficients are therefore excluded. PDF p. 10 (printed p. 174), Data analysis; PDF p. 12 (printed p. 176), Tables 5-6.

open_items: The paper states averaging across raters but does not explain how the requested solutions were aggregated into each observation in Table 2. The analysis unit, SD level and independent unit underlying the Wilcoxon uncertainty are consequently unconfirmed (PDF p. 8, printed p. 172, CPS performance; PDF p. 10, printed p. 174, Data analysis; PDF p. 11, printed p. 175, Table 2).

Only the overall final analyzed sample is explicitly printed. Table 2 gives no condition-specific or outcome-specific valid participant-pair counts; these estimate counts remain null. The paper does not print a separate aggregate randomized count, and none is calculated from sequence counts (PDF p. 5, printed p. 169, Participants; PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp. 172-173, Procedure and Figure 3; PDF p. 11, printed p. 175, Table 2).
No first-round or sequence-specific creativity statistics are reported; only paired condition contrasts can be extracted from this paper.

The procedure describes the other sequence completing tasks in reverse order, whereas Figure 3 labels PIT 1 then PIT 2 in both sequences while reversing AI feedback. Actual product order and product-by-condition mapping need clarification (PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp. 172-173).

Cohen’s r is reported without its calculation formula, standardizer or confidence-interval method. Its sign convention is not explained; the printed negative signs cannot uniformly indicate lower personalised-condition performance because quality and elaboration have higher personalised means (PDF p. 11, printed p. 175, Table 2).

Exact participant overlap with c041 is unconfirmed. The reconciled screening form flags probable overlap based on matching primary-source reports; sample deduplication requires confirmation before treating the reports as independent.
The release year and exact snapshot of the GPT-4-based systems are not stated in the paper (PDF p. 5, printed p. 169, GenAI feedback conditions).
notes: Extraction date: 2026-10-10. The complete markdown was read from start to end, including references and Appendix Tables A1-A2. Every cited PDF page was checked with PyMuPDF text extraction; Figure 3 was also inspected visually to confirm random assignment of feedback sequence. There is one study and one reported paired AI-configuration contrast for each of three scored output dimensions. No first-round, no-AI, across-people or after-AI outcome contrast is reported. The study-level final sample is retained, but no outcome-specific count is inferred from it or from test statistics. All statistics and signs are transcribed as printed; original numerical precision is preserved in the PDF row quotes. No effect, difference, standard error, sample count or model year was calculated or supplied from outside the paper.
